source.title_on_document: AI-Augmented Brainwriting: Investigating the use of LLMs in group ideation

supplement.where: Supplementary Information cited on p. 8, section 3.3, and p. 15, section 5.2.3; no URL provided. It is not included in the supplied PDF or markdown.
supplement.holds: Evaluation-engine prompt and rating-scale explanations (Supplementary Information Figure 1), and the full semantic-cluster and corresponding-term lists.

paper_design_summary: Sixteen college students in five project teams completed a fixed sequence of individual brainwriting followed by GPT-3-assisted group ideation, selection and development (pp. 8-10, sections 4-4.2). The resulting idea corpus was assessed through student self-ratings, semantic analysis, and later ratings by three HCI experts, six novice designers and GPT-4 (pp. 10-11, sections 4.2-5.1; p. 17, section 5.3). The later evaluation-engine comparison reused this corpus and did not supply an additional AI-assistance condition to the students (p. 17, section 5.3).

studies.label: Course-based group-AI brainwriting and subsequent evaluation of the same idea corpus

assignment.what_was_assigned: All students followed the same prescribed sequence: individual ideas without AI first, then group ideation and development with GPT-3. These are repeated phases for the same people, not separately allocated groups. Random ordering mentioned later concerns ideas presented to evaluators, not assignment of AI assistance.
assignment.quote: They first generated ideas independently, then worked with their team members to co-create ideas with GPT-3, and finally, chose ideas as a team to further develop through collaboration with GPT-3.
assignment.locator: p. 8, section 4 (fixed sequence); p. 9, section 4.1 (teams and implementation); p. 11, section 5.1 (random presentation order of ideas only)

arms.name: Initial individual brainwriting without AI
arms.description: Students wrote their own ideas on their team Conceptboard before using GPT-3. The people count is the same cohort that subsequently received AI assistance (pp. 8-9, sections 4-4.1).

arms.name: Subsequent GPT-3-assisted group brainwriting
arms.description: The same students prompted GPT-3 for additional ideas and collaboratively developed and selected ideas. The paper distinguishes GPT-3-generated and collaboratively-generated outputs within this phase; counts across phases must not be added (pp. 8-10, sections 4-4.2 and Table 1).

participants.who: College students enrolled in an advanced undergraduate tangible interaction design course, working in five project teams. The expert and novice evaluators are raters, not additional idea-generating participants.
participants.quote: In February 2023, we conducted a 70-minutes Brainwriting session with 16 college students (0 men, ages 18-23) who were enrolled in an advanced undergraduate course on tangible interaction design.
participants.locator: p. 8, section 4.1 (student cohort); p. 9, section 4.1 (five project teams); p. 10, Table 1 (all teams); p. 12, section 5.2.1 (all students responded, n=16); p. 11, section 5.1 (separate evaluators)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI Playground GPT-3 for ideation; GPT-4 for subsequent evaluation
ai_tool.how_used: Teams repeatedly prompted GPT-3 to generate additional ideas and elaborate their own ideas, then copied ideas to Conceptboard and selected and developed project concepts (pp. 9-10, section 4.1). GPT-4 rated the same ideas only after students had chosen final ideas; its ratings were not available to students during ideation (p. 17, section 5.3; p. 20, section 5.3.3).

task.description: Develop a novel tangible user interface supporting productivity, creativity and well-being for people working or studying in mobile environments, then choose and develop a semester-project idea (p. 9, section 4.1).

outcomes.name: Innovation of ideas (students' self-ratings)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: At the end of the Brainwriting session, students rated their own, GPT-3-generated and collaborative ideas on a Likert scale to narrow the idea pool (p. 10, section 4.2). Table 2 labels these self-ratings and reports Avg and Std by idea source. The number of student ratings is not stated; n_units remains null. The cohort and evaluated-corpus counts cannot be substituted for that unknown rating count. The scored ideas were produced during the same session.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Collaboratively-Generated ideas from subsequent GPT-3-assisted group brainwriting
contrasts.control_arm: Human-Generated ideas from initial individual brainwriting without AI
contrasts.reported: Students' self-ratings of innovation: Collab Avg 4.81, Std 0.40 versus Human Avg 4.31, Std 0.70; GPT-3-generated ideas separately received Avg 4.25, Std 0.68. These are descriptive ratings of idea sources from the same cohort, not independent expert ratings or a randomized assistance contrast; no inferential test for the assistance comparison is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, section 4.2 and Table 2, Innovation columns, Human, GPT-3 and Collab rows

outcomes.name: Semantic clusters in human-generated and GPT-3-generated idea pools
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Analysis aggregates all five Conceptboards. spaCy extracts nouns and adjectives; spaCy and Gensim are also used for topic modeling (p. 11, section 5.1). GPT-4 performs semantic analysis, yielding clusters for pooled Human-Generated (H) and GPT-3-Generated (G) ideas (p. 12, section 5.1; pp. 14-15, section 5.2.3). The accompanying LPA analysis uses normalized term-frequency vectors and symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence relative to a joint corpus to identify overused, underused and missing terms (pp. 11-12, section 5.1 and Equation 1; pp. 15-16, section 5.2.3 and Figure 4). This is a comparison of idea-source pools; question remains none.

contrasts.reported: Human-generated ideas (H): 20 semantic clusters; GPT-3-generated ideas (G): 21 clusters; 12 similar clusters contained shared terms. This compares pooled human and model idea sources, not diversity between separately allocated AI-assisted and unassisted groups of people; no inferential test is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 14, section 5.2.3, Semantic clustering analysis; p. 15, continuation; pp. 11-12, section 5.1 and Equation 1 (methods and two source documents); p. 16, Figure 4 (LPA)

diversity_detail.metric: Semantic cluster counts and clusters with shared terms; accompanying LPA term signatures based on symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence of normalized term-frequency distributions.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Not stated. GPT-4 is named for semantic analysis, but no embedding model is specified (p. 12, section 5.1).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Two pooled source documents, Human-Generated (H) and GPT-3-Generated (G), aggregated across the five Conceptboards (pp. 11-12, section 5.1). n_units=2 counts source pools. Semantic clusters are compared between H and G (pp. 14-15, section 5.2.3). LPA compares each source frequency vector with the joint corpus; there is no pairwise comparison of separately assigned participants or assistance arms.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No standard errors, confidence intervals or inferential tests are reported for the semantic-cluster counts or LPA source-pool comparison (pp. 14-16, section 5.2.3 and Figure 4).
diversity_detail.notes: Human-Generated ideas yield 20 clusters and GPT-3-Generated ideas 21; 12 similar clusters share terms (p. 14, section 5.2.3). LPA distinguishes overused, underused and missing terms rather than providing an AI-assistance diversity effect (pp. 15-16, section 5.2.3 and Figure 4). Full cluster and corresponding-term lists are in separately cited Supplementary Information, absent from this PDF (p. 15).

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideas on the Conceptboards are counted separately by Human-Generated, GPT-3-Generated and Collaboratively-Generated source within each of the five teams (p. 9, section 4.1; p. 10, Table 1). n_units counts the teams tabulated, not people. The whole evaluated corpus contains 148 ideas (p. 17, section 5.3.2); neither that corpus count nor the per-team idea counts are participant counts. These descriptive source counts do not isolate an effect of AI assistance.

outcomes.name: Relevance of ideas (Expert evaluation; all sources pooled)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Relevance assesses connection with or appropriateness for the problem statement (p. 8, section 3.3). The reported expert evaluation uses three HCI researchers who rated all ideas; a fourth reviewer rated only a subset and was excluded from the reported evaluation (p. 11, section 5.1). All evaluators used the same definitions and scale anchors on a 1 to 5 Likert scale (p. 17, section 5.3). The paper describes a per-idea score averaged within each evaluator group (p. 18, section 5.3.2(a)); n_units=148 denotes the common evaluated idea corpus, not ratings or people. Table 4 reports Avg and Stdev in the Average over all ideas column and also presents ratings for the chosen project ideas by team. The Stdev aggregation basis in the all-idea column is not further specified. The all-idea summaries pool Human-Generated, GPT-3-Generated and Collaboratively-Generated ideas, with no source-specific assistance contrast. Output timing is immediate because these ideas were produced in the original Brainwriting session; later evaluation did not create new participant outputs or an after-AI condition (p. 17, section 5.3; p. 20, section 5.3.3).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Possible overlapping course/sample report: the separate paper described as currently under review for a different conference about integrating this framework into a tangible interaction course and about students' reflections and learning. This passage does not identify the paper bibliographically or confirm the exact participant overlap.
sample_overlap.quote: In a separate paper [currently under review for a different conference], we contextualized the use of this framework within a broader integration of generative AI into a tangible interaction course, and discussed students’ reflections and learning.

eligibility.reason: The same class completed a fixed sequence of no-AI individual ideation and GPT-3-assisted group ideation; assistance and condition order were not randomly assigned (p. 8, section 4; pp. 9-10, section 4.1). The cohort contains 16 idea-generating students, below 50 (p. 8, section 4.1; p. 12, section 5.2.1). Independent expert, novice and GPT-4 ratings score relevance, innovation and insightfulness on the actual outputs, so criterion 3 is met independently of student self-ratings (p. 17, section 5.3; p. 20, Table 4). The 148 evaluated ideas are outputs from this same study, not additional participants; the three experts and six novices are evaluators (p. 11, section 5.1; p. 17, sections 5.3 and 5.3.2). Random presentation order for reviewers does not randomize human AI assistance (p. 11, section 5.1). Retain as observational context for the nonrandom within-group comparison; pooled evaluator summaries and human-versus-model source comparisons are descriptive and do not estimate an assistance effect.

one_line_finding: In a fixed-sequence exercise with 16 students (p. 8, sections 4-4.1), collaborative ideas received higher student innovation self-ratings (Avg 4.81, Std 0.40) than initial human-generated ideas (Avg 4.31, Std 0.70; p. 10, Table 2), without a randomized test of AI assistance.
notes: The outcome list separates student self-ratings, source-pool counts and length, source-pool semantic analysis, and the expert, novice and GPT-4 evaluations of the same ideas. All evaluator-specific n_units values refer to the same 148-output corpus, which must not be counted repeatedly or added to the participant cohort. Student rating counts remain unknown. Empty statistics_available arrays for descriptive records mean that no listed inferential assistance-contrast statistics or complete arm-specific means/SDs/sample-size combination are being claimed; the printed descriptive values are retained in reported. Evaluator agreement, ranking correlations, prompt categories and student perceptions of the process are not additional creative-output effects. Table 4 selected-project ratings are secondary summaries of the same relevance, innovation and insightfulness outcomes, not additional outcome constructs. The separately cited Supplementary Information is not present in the local PDF.
